course.title: Introduction to Robotics
course.description: A concept-first tour of how robots sense, think, and move — the sense-plan-act loop, sensors and actuators, feedback control, coordinate frames and kinematics, and autonomy with safety. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare's Introduction to Robotics (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). No specific hardware required.

questions.prompt: A robot's basic operating cycle is best summarized as…
questions.explanation: Sense (gather data), plan (decide), act (move) — the organizing loop of the whole course.

questions.prompt: A device that lets a robot perceive its environment is a…
questions.explanation: Sensors turn physical quantities (distance, angle, light) into signals the robot can read.

questions.prompt: A device that converts energy into motion is an…
questions.explanation: Actuators — motors, servos — produce the movement.

questions.prompt: In a feedback control loop, the 'error' is…
questions.explanation: Error = target (setpoint) − what you actually measured. Control shrinks it toward zero.

questions.prompt: A wheel encoder primarily measures…
options: how far/fast the wheel has turned
questions.explanation: Encoders count wheel rotation, letting the robot estimate distance and speed.

questions.prompt: A gear train that reduces output speed typically…
questions.explanation: Gearing trades speed for torque — slower but stronger (ideally, ignoring friction losses).

questions.prompt: Path planning is the task of…
options: finding a route from start to goal while avoiding obstacles
questions.explanation: Planning searches for a safe, feasible path through the robot's space.

questions.prompt: A core safety rule for a robot working near people is to…
options: limit force/speed and provide an emergency stop
questions.explanation: Bounded force/speed plus a reliable stop keep people safe around moving machines.

lessons.title: What a robot is: the sense-plan-act loop
lessons.grammar_note: Keep the loop in order: sense → plan → act, then repeat.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define a robot and describe the sense-plan-act loop that drives it. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which three words summarize a robot's cycle?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A robot is a machine that *senses* its world, *decides* what to do, and *acts* to change something physical — then repeats. That loop is called *sense-plan-act*. Sensing turns the world into numbers (a distance, an angle). Planning uses those numbers to choose an action. Acting drives actuators to move. A purely *reactive* robot skips deliberate planning and maps sensing straight to action (sense-act); a *deliberative* robot builds a model and plans over it. Most real robots blend both.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A floor robot approaching a wall: SENSE — a range sensor reads 0.20 m ahead. PLAN — rule says 'if distance < 0.30 m, turn'. ACT — command the wheels to rotate in place. On the next loop it senses 0.60 m of clear space and plans 'drive forward'. The same three steps run over and over, many times per second.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each step as sense, plan, or act: (1) a camera reports a red ball at the left, (2) the controller decides to steer left, (3) the left motor slows so the robot curves, (4) an encoder reports the wheel turned 2 revolutions. Answers: (1) sense, (2) plan, (3) act, (4) sense.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a robot must look humanlike — a thermostat-driven conveyor is a simple robot. Mistake: thinking the loop runs once; it repeats continuously. Exit: (a) Name the three steps in order. (b) Which step reads the world? Answers: sense-plan-act; sense.

lessons.title: Sensors: how robots perceive
lessons.grammar_note: Proprioceptive = about the robot's own body; exteroceptive = about the outside world.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify common robot sensors and estimate a distance from a range sensor. Warm-up: which sensor tells a robot how far its own wheel has turned?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Sensors convert physical quantities into signals. *Proprioceptive* sensors measure the robot's own state: wheel *encoders* (rotation), an *IMU* (acceleration and turning). *Exteroceptive* sensors measure the outside world: cameras (light), ultrasonic and LiDAR range finders (distance), bump switches (contact). Every sensor is noisy and limited, so robots usually combine several — a step called *sensor fusion* — rather than trusting any single reading.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: An ultrasonic sensor measures distance by *time of flight*: it emits a pulse and times the echo. Distance = (speed_of_sound × echo_time) / 2, halved because the pulse travels out and back. With sound at about 343 m/s and an echo returning in 0.010 s: distance = (343 × 0.010) / 2 = 3.43 / 2 = 1.715 m. So the object is roughly 1.7 m away.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as proprioceptive or exteroceptive: (1) wheel encoder, (2) forward-facing camera, (3) IMU measuring tilt, (4) ultrasonic range finder. Then: if an echo returns in 0.004 s, about how far is the object? Answers: (1) proprioceptive, (2) exteroceptive, (3) proprioceptive, (4) exteroceptive; distance = (343 × 0.004)/2 ≈ 0.69 m.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting to halve the time-of-flight distance (the pulse makes a round trip). Mistake: trusting one noisy reading instead of fusing several. Exit: (a) Encoder — proprioceptive or exteroceptive? (b) Why divide the echo distance by two? Answers: proprioceptive; the pulse travels to the object and back.

lessons.title: Actuators and motors: how robots move
lessons.grammar_note: Gearing rule: speed down means torque up (same power, minus losses).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name common actuators and use a gear ratio to trade speed for torque. Warm-up: what does a gearbox give you when it slows a motor down?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Actuators* convert stored energy into motion. A *DC motor* spins continuously and is fast but weak at the shaft; a *servo* holds a commanded angle; a *stepper* moves in fixed increments for open-loop positioning. Two quantities matter: *speed* (how fast it turns) and *torque* (how hard it can twist). A *gear ratio* trades one for the other. For a reduction ratio N:1, output speed = input speed / N and output torque ≈ input torque × N (ignoring friction). Power — roughly speed × torque — is conserved, so you cannot get more of both for free.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A motor spins at 100 rpm and delivers 0.10 N·m of torque. Put it behind a 5:1 reduction gearbox. Output speed = 100 / 5 = 20 rpm. Output torque ≈ 0.10 × 5 = 0.50 N·m. The wheel now turns five times slower but can push about five times harder — useful for climbing a ramp.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: A motor runs at 200 rpm with 0.04 N·m through a 4:1 reduction. (1) Output speed? (2) Output torque? (3) Did torque go up or down? Answers: (1) 200/4 = 50 rpm, (2) 0.04 × 4 = 0.16 N·m, (3) up.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting a gearbox to raise speed AND torque at once — it trades them. Mistake: confusing a servo (holds an angle) with a plain DC motor (spins freely). Exit: (a) A 3:1 reduction does what to output speed? (b) …to output torque? Answers: divides it by 3; multiplies it by about 3.

questions.prompt: The correct order of the core robot loop is…
questions.explanation: Sense, then plan, then act — repeated.

questions.prompt: An ultrasonic range sensor measures distance using…
options: time of flight of an echo
questions.explanation: It times the pulse's round trip and halves it.

questions.prompt: A wheel encoder is an example of a … sensor.
questions.explanation: It reports the robot's own wheel motion.

questions.prompt: A 5:1 reduction gearbox turns 100 rpm input into…
questions.explanation: Output speed = input / 5 = 20 rpm.

questions.prompt: An actuator's job is to…
questions.explanation: Actuators produce movement.

questions.prompt: A forward-facing camera is a … sensor.
questions.explanation: It senses the outside world.

lessons.title: Control loops: feedback and PID intuition
lessons.grammar_note: Error = setpoint − measurement. Every control term acts on that error.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace a feedback loop and explain what the P, I, and D terms each do. Warm-up: if the target speed is 100 and you measure 60, what is the error?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
*Feedback control* keeps a measured value near a *setpoint*. Each cycle it computes error = setpoint − measurement and sends a correction to the actuator. A *proportional* (P) term reacts to the *current* error — bigger error, bigger push. An *integral* (I) term sums *past* error to erase a stubborn steady-state gap. A *derivative* (D) term reacts to how fast the error is *changing*, damping overshoot. Together they form a *PID controller*: command = Kp·error + Ki·(sum of error) + Kd·(rate of change of error). Pseudocode:
```
integral = 0
prev_error = 0
loop every dt:
    error = setpoint - measure()
    integral = integral + error * dt
    derivative = (error - prev_error) / dt
    command = Kp*error + Ki*integral + Kd*derivative
    set_motor(command)
    prev_error = error
```

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Trace a proportional-only speed controller with setpoint = 100 and Kp = 0.5.
Step 1: measure 60 → error = 40 → command = 0.5 × 40 = 20 (push hard, speeds up).
Step 2: measure 90 → error = 10 → command = 0.5 × 10 = 5 (ease off).
Step 3: measure 98 → error = 2 → command = 0.5 × 2 = 1 (gentle nudge).
The error shrinks 40 → 10 → 2, so the speed settles near the setpoint. That is stable feedback: the correction fades as the error does.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Same P-controller, setpoint = 100, Kp = 0.5. (1) Measured 80 → error and command? (2) Measured 95 → error and command? (3) Is the error growing or shrinking across those steps? Answers: (1) error 20, command 10; (2) error 5, command 2.5; (3) shrinking — the loop is converging.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing error as measurement − setpoint (sign flips and the loop pushes the wrong way). Mistake: thinking the P term alone always reaches the target exactly — a constant load can leave a small steady-state error that the I term removes. Exit: (a) What removes steady-state error? (b) What does the D term respond to? Answers: the integral term; the rate of change of the error.

lessons.title: Coordinate frames and basic kinematics
lessons.grammar_note: A pose has a rotation AND a translation — you need both to place a point.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain robot vs world frames and compute how far a wheel carries the robot. Warm-up: how far does one full turn of a wheel move the robot along the ground?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
Positions are always measured relative to a *frame*. The *world frame* is fixed to the room; the *robot frame* moves with the robot. A point known in the robot frame is placed in the world frame by first *rotating* by the robot's heading θ, then *translating* by the robot's position (tx, ty):
x_world = x_robot·cos θ − y_robot·sin θ + tx
y_world = x_robot·sin θ + y_robot·cos θ + ty.
For driving, a rolling wheel of radius r covers 2πr of ground per full revolution — this is *forward kinematics* for a wheel: turning the wheels predicts where the robot goes.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Wheel-distance: a wheel of radius r = 0.04 m makes 5 full revolutions. Distance = 2·π·r·revolutions = 2 × 3.1416 × 0.04 × 5 ≈ 1.257 m. Frame check: a landmark sits at (1, 0) in the robot frame; the robot is at world position (2, 3) with heading θ = 0. Then x_world = 1·cos0 − 0·sin0 + 2 = 3, y_world = 1·sin0 + 0·cos0 + 3 = 3, so the landmark is at (3, 3) in the world.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) A wheel of radius 0.05 m turns 3 revolutions — distance? (2) With heading θ = 90°, a point at (1, 0) in the robot frame, robot at world (0, 0): what is x_world (use cos90 = 0, sin90 = 1)? Answers: (1) 2π × 0.05 × 3 ≈ 0.94 m; (2) x_world = 1·cos90 − 0·sin90 + 0 = 0 (the point rotates onto the world y-axis).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: adding the translation but forgetting to rotate first (order matters: rotate, then translate). Mistake: using diameter instead of radius in 2πr. Exit: (a) One wheel revolution moves the robot how far? (b) Which comes first, rotation or translation? Answers: 2πr; rotation.

items.example: The speed setpoint was 100, so the controller pushed until the error was near zero.

items.translation: the geometry of motion — how joint or wheel movement maps to where the robot ends up

items.example: Path planning routed the robot around the chair to the door.

questions.prompt: In a control loop, error is defined as…
questions.explanation: Target minus what you measured; the loop drives it to zero.

questions.prompt: The proportional (P) term responds to the…
questions.explanation: P reacts to the present error — bigger error, bigger push.

questions.prompt: The integral (I) term mainly helps remove…
questions.explanation: Summing past error erases a stubborn constant gap.

questions.prompt: A wheel of radius r moves the robot how far per full revolution?
questions.explanation: The circumference 2πr rolls out in one revolution.

questions.prompt: Placing a robot-frame point into the world frame requires…
questions.explanation: Rotate by the heading, then add the robot's position.

questions.prompt: The derivative (D) term responds to the…
options: rate of change of the error
questions.explanation: D reacts to how fast the error is changing, damping overshoot.

lessons.title: Applied project: design a simple robot for a task

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: On paper, design a simple autonomous robot for one concrete job — for example, a robot that drives to a doorway while avoiding obstacles, or one that follows a line across a room. You will not build hardware; you will specify the sensors, actuators, and control logic clearly enough that someone else could implement it.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the task and success condition in one sentence. 2) Sensors: list which sensors it needs and what each measures (e.g. an ultrasonic sensor for obstacle distance, encoders for how far it has driven). 3) Actuators: name the motors/servos and what motion they produce. 4) Control logic: write the sense-plan-act loop in a few lines of pseudocode, using a clear error rule or if-then decision (e.g. 'if distance < 0.3 m, turn; else drive forward'). 5) Autonomy & safety: name one way it plans a path around an obstacle, and one safety measure (bounded speed, an emergency stop, or a bump switch that halts the motors).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The task and success condition are specific and testable. ✔ Every sensor is justified by something the robot must know. ✔ Every actuator maps to a required motion. ✔ The control loop is a valid sense-plan-act cycle with a correct error or decision rule (error = setpoint − measurement, not reversed). ✔ You named a path-planning idea and a concrete safety measure. If all five hold, you've designed like a roboticist.
